name: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder

ethnicAssociations: Higher prevalence in East Asian populations
Higher prevalence in African and Afro-Caribbean populations

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: 2015 International Panel for NMO Diagnosis (IPND) Criteria

criteria.description: At least one core clinical characteristic: optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy/diencephalic syndrome, or symptomatic cerebral syndrome
Positive AQP4-IgG serology (for AQP4-IgG seropositive NMOSD)
For seronegative NMOSD: at least 2 core clinical characteristics with specific additional MRI requirements and dissemination in space
MOG-IgG antibody positivity (identifies MOG antibody-associated disease subset)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: AQP4-IgG positive: at least 1 core clinical characteristic plus positive AQP4-IgG. AQP4-IgG negative: at least 2 core clinical characteristics with additional MRI criteria.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: MOG-IgG associated disease is increasingly recognized as a separate entity from AQP4-positive NMOSD.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Neuronal loss in central nervous system

laboratory: AQP4-IgG (aquaporin-4) antibodies positive (present in ~75-80% of NMOSD)
MOG-IgG antibodies (identifies a related but distinct subset)
CSF pleocytosis often >50 cells/uL with neutrophilic predominance
CSF oligoclonal bands less common than MS (~15-30%)
Elevated CSF GFAP levels during attacks
imaging: Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>3 vertebral segments) on spinal MRI
Central cord lesion (H-shaped or holocord) pattern
Long optic nerve lesions (>50% of nerve length) or chiasmal involvement
Brain MRI may be normal or show non-MS pattern lesions
Periependymal lesions around third and fourth ventricles
genetic: No single causative gene; complex genetic susceptibility
other: Visual evoked potentials may show absent or severely delayed responses
Optical coherence tomography showing severe retinal nerve fiber layer thinning

distinguishingFeatures: MS typically has shorter spinal cord lesions (<2 segments)
MS has periventricular ovoid lesions (Dawson fingers)
MS has oligoclonal bands in >95% vs ~20% in NMOSD
MS has less severe attacks with better recovery
AE primarily affects cortex with psychiatric features
AE has specific neural antibodies (NMDA-R, LGI1, etc.)
AE does not typically cause optic neuritis or myelitis
Sarcoidosis involves systemic organs (lungs, lymph nodes, skin)
Elevated serum ACE levels in sarcoidosis

redFlags: Respiratory failure during myelitis attack requires urgent intervention
Severe visual loss to no light perception suggests NMOSD over MS
Failure to respond to MS disease-modifying therapies
Some MS drugs (interferons, natalizumab) can worsen NMOSD
Intractable hiccups or vomiting lasting >48 hours should prompt NMOSD workup
Complete transverse myelitis more suggestive of NMOSD than MS
references: Wingerchuk DM, et al. International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders. Neurology. 2015;85(2):177-189.
Pittock SJ, et al. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Lancet. 2023;401(10374):336-349.
Jarius S, et al. Neuromyelitis optica. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2020;6(1):85.
